entries.title: Where to file a consumer complaint (Consumer Protection Act, 2019)
entries.text: A consumer can file a complaint for defective goods, deficient services, unfair trade practices or overcharging. District Consumer Commission handles claims up to Rs 50 lakh; State Commission Rs 50 lakh to Rs 2 crore; National Commission above Rs 2 crore (value of goods/services paid). Complaints can be filed online on e-Daakhil. No court-fee for claims up to Rs 5 lakh. A lawyer is not mandatory.
entries.cite: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (filing; pecuniary limits per 2021 Rules)

entries.title: Time limit for consumer complaints
entries.text: A consumer complaint must generally be filed within 2 years from the date the cause of action arose. Late complaints can be admitted only if the Commission records sufficient cause for delay.

entries.title: Pre-litigation step: National Consumer Helpline
entries.text: Before filing, the person can lodge a grievance with the National Consumer Helpline (phone 1915, or consumerhelpline.gov.in); many refund disputes are settled with the company at this stage. A written complaint to the seller's grievance officer, and a legal notice, are sensible first steps.
entries.cite: National Consumer Helpline (Dept. of Consumer Affairs)

entries.title: Rental security deposit not returned
entries.text: There is no single central law on deposits. Rent and deposit rules are mostly state-specific (state Rent Control Acts), and the rental agreement terms matter most. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 is only a model for states and applies only where a state has adopted it. Usual path: demand in writing -> legal notice giving a deadline (commonly 15 days) -> civil suit for recovery of money (a summary suit under Order XXXVII CPC is possible for a fixed sum due under a written agreement). Money-recovery suits are generally subject to a 3-year limitation period.
entries.cite: State Rent Control Act (varies); Limitation Act, 1963; Order XXXVII, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

entries.title: Unpaid salary / wages
entries.text: Unpaid wages can be raised with the employer in writing first, then with the Labour Commissioner / labour office of the state. India is moving from the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 to the Code on Wages, 2019; which one applies to a given case depends on commencement and the person's wage level and sector, so this must be checked. For employees whose wage claim is a pure contract dispute (e.g. senior managers), a civil suit or legal notice may be the route. Evidence: appointment letter, salary slips, bank statements, emails/WhatsApp about dues.
entries.cite: Payment of Wages Act, 1936 / Code on Wages, 2019 (applicability to be verified)

entries.title: Cheque bounce
entries.text: If a cheque is dishonoured, the payee must send a written demand notice to the drawer within 30 days of receiving the bank's return memo. The drawer then has 15 days from receiving the notice to pay. If unpaid, a criminal complaint can be filed in court within 1 month after those 15 days end.

entries.title: What a legal notice is
entries.text: A legal notice is a formal written demand stating the facts, the amount or action demanded, and a deadline, before going to court/forum. It is usually not mandatory for consumer complaints, but is useful evidence that the other side was given a chance to settle. Send by registered post/speed post with acknowledgement and also by email; keep proof of dispatch.

entries.title: Free legal aid
entries.text: Free legal services are available to eligible persons (e.g. women, children, SC/ST, persons in custody, and persons below an income limit set by the state) through the State/District Legal Services Authority. National helpline: 15100.

entries.title: Criminal law renumbering
entries.text: From 1 July 2024 the Indian Penal Code, CrPC and Evidence Act were replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam. Old IPC/CrPC section numbers must not be quoted for new matters.

escalate_message: This looks like something where a real lawyer (or the District Legal Services Authority, free legal aid helpline 15100) should be involved before you act. I can still help you organise your facts and documents to take to them.
